name: Nebraska
$methodComment: REUSES Vermont's existing bracketPerPeriodAllowance() dispatch DIRECTLY — no new function needed. An earlier pass this session left this on a custom 'bracket_annual_from_period_allowance' method because the per-period tables extracted garbled under pdftotext -layout and only the ANNUAL table survived; CLOSED properly this session by re-extracting the SAME pages WITHOUT -layout (the fix already proven for NY/OH elsewhere in this project) — every one of Circular EN's own published per-period tables (daily/weekly/biweekly/semimonthly/monthly/quarterly/semiannual/annual) came out cleanly and was verified internally to the cent by chaining each bracket's base from the one below. With the REAL per-period tables in hand, Nebraska's shape is now IDENTICAL to Vermont's (subtract a flat per-allowance amount from PER-PERIOD wages, look up a bracket table published for that exact period) — reusing bracketPerPeriodAllowance() rather than keeping a bespoke annualize-then-divide approximation function around. The custom nebraskaWithholding() function and its 'bracket_annual_from_period_allowance' method were REMOVED from state.ts in the same pass that fixed this file, so the dead approximation code doesn't linger once the real data made it unnecessary.

$importantDistinctionFromReturnBrackets: Nebraska's REAL statutory individual income tax return brackets (Neb. Rev. Stat. 77-2715.03) are a DIFFERENT, simpler 3-tier schedule (2.46% / 3.51% / 4.55% top rate for 2026) that several secondary sources conflated with the withholding table below. This is the SAME structural distinction Wisconsin's data file already documents in this project: the WITHHOLDING table (Circular EN) is what payroll actually uses, and it is NOT required to match the RETURN bracket schedule exactly — Circular EN's own 6-step schedule (topping out at 4.60%, not 4.55%) is a genuinely different, independently-published table, not a transcription error. This file uses the Circular EN withholding table, correctly.

bracketPerPeriodAllowance.allowanceAmountComment: Value of ONE withholding allowance, multiplied by the number of allowances claimed on Nebraska Form W-4N (or the employee's federal W-4 allowance count for pre-2020 certificates still on file — Circular EN explicitly grandfathers pre-2020 federal W-4s the same way this project's other post-2020-redesign states, e.g. Delaware, do), then SUBTRACTED from wages BEFORE the bracket lookup — a deduction, not a post-tax credit (the opposite of Delaware's shape built earlier this project).
bracketPerPeriodAllowance.bracketsComment: 'Single' schedule is labelled 'SINGLE Person-Including Head of Household' and 'Married' is 'MARRIED Person-Including Surviving Spouse' in Circular EN's own table headers — i.e. Nebraska's own withholding table explicitly folds HOH into single (not this engine's usual disclosed simplification; the source says so directly, the same rare case Kansas's KW-100 was). EVERY one of Circular EN's 8 published per-period tables is now recorded here VERBATIM (not derived from the annual figure) — daily/weekly/biweekly/semimonthly/monthly/quarterly/semiannual/annual, both statuses. This SUPERSEDES an earlier version of this file that only had the annual table and derived the rest by division; that approximation is no longer needed or used now that the real tables are in hand. One cross-check worth keeping on record: the QUARTERLY table's own printed base at the $10,033 boundary is 243.24, while dividing the ANNUAL table's corresponding base (972.93) by 4 gives 243.2325, which rounds to 243.23 — a one-cent difference between the real published table and what naive division would have produced, exactly the kind of drift that would have gone unnoticed had the approximation been kept instead of replaced.

supplementalComment: Circular EN: if supplemental wages (bonus, commission, overtime, severance, sales awards) are paid WITH regular wages, treat the total as one payment through the normal formula. If paid separately, either (a) aggregate with the current or immediately preceding period's regular wages and net out tax already withheld — the engine's default — or (b) withhold a flat 3.5% (notably NOT Nebraska's top marginal rate of 4.60%, unlike most other states' flat-supplemental conventions in this project), computed by flatRateSupplementalFromConfig() only when the employer elects it (input.employer.supplementalFlatRateElection).
exemptComment: Nebraska has ROLLING conformity to the Internal Revenue Code (confirmed via a cross-source search, consistent with Nebraska's own Form W-4N instructions using federal AGI as the withholding-relevant starting point) — the same 'starts from federal AGI, no addback for these categories' inference tier as Wisconsin/Ohio, not yet upgraded to a direct statute or Circular EN quote naming each category.

reciprocity.rule: NONE. Nebraska does not have reciprocity agreements with any bordering state (Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Colorado, Wyoming, South Dakota) — cross-source confirmed, not independently verified against Circular EN's own text this session (the document's Table of Contents does not list a reciprocity section, consistent with 'none' but not a direct quote either).

localIncomeTax.rule: NONE. No Nebraska city or county levies a local income or wage tax.

verification: PROVEN via calculatePaycheck() against the REAL per-period tables (not an approximation): (1) 0 allowances, weekly $500, landing in one weekly bracket. (2) 2 allowances shifting the net figure into the prior weekly bracket — this fixture caught a genuine hand-arithmetic error of the AUTHOR's own during this session (27,716 x 3.22% was first miscalculated as 892.6552 instead of the correct 892.4552, a 20-cent slip that would have shipped a wrong test assertion, $10.35 instead of the correct $10.34, had the test suite not caught the mismatch on first run — corrected before commit). (3) quarterly $9,000, chosen SPECIFICALLY because it produces a different cent answer ($290.96) under the real per-period table than the old annualize-then-divide approximation would have ($290.98) — this fixture exists to catch a regression back to the approximation, not just to exercise the happy path. See tests/engine.test.ts, describe('Nebraska'). No official Circular EN worked example was ever found to reproduce verbatim, so all fixtures are hand/script-derived against this file's own verified tables, not source-published answers — but the tables themselves are now the REAL published ones, not a derived approximation.
knownGaps: Descriptive notes carried from the 2026 file (reciprocity, local-tax rules, method comments) were checked against the 2025 source for the fields this engine computes from; narrative text that only describes 2026 history should be read as background.

suiEmployer.$comment: Normalized employer-side unemployment parameters — the shape src/taxes/state.ts reads. The detailed unemploymentInsurance block above stays the record of research; this exists because that block's shape varies too much between states to compute from directly (wage bases as objects, industry-keyed rate maps, differently-named keys).

supplementalWages.source: Circular EN, per this file's supplementalComment: a bonus paid WITH regular wages is treated as one payment through the normal formula; paid separately, the employer may either aggregate and net out, or withhold a flat 3.5%. Notably NOT Nebraska's top marginal rate (4.60%), unlike most states' flat-supplemental conventions.

supplementalAggregation.source: Circular EN: paid separately, the employer may either aggregate with the current or immediately preceding period's regular wages and net out tax already withheld, or withhold a flat 3.5%.
supplementalAggregation.engineNote: Wired via aggregateWithPriorRegularPayment(): the caller supplies input.priorRegularPayment (that cheque's taxable wages and the state tax withheld from it), and a bonus paid on its own cheque is taxed on the combined figure less what was already withheld, floored at zero. Nothing changes when the caller omits it.

$yearNote: 2025 ruleset: Circular EN percentage tables for wages paid on or after 1 January 2025 (2.26% to 5.37%, top bracket above $72,750 single / $80,040 married a year) and a $2,360 annual withholding allowance (2026: 5.2% top, $2,440). Supplemental wages paid separately may be withheld at 5% (2026: 3.5%).
